# Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Human Health and Diseases fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Immune system — innate and adaptive immunity

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The immune system is the body's defence network, arranged in layers. **Innate immunity** is inborn, non-specific and immediate — barriers, phagocytes, inflammation. **Adaptive (acquired) immunity** is specific to each antigen, learns, remembers, and is carried by lymphocytes (B and T cells). Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) kills infected cells; humoral immunity (B cells → antibodies) neutralises free pathogens.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — the layers of defence (study in this order)**

| Step | Layer | What it does | Speed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Physical / chemical barriers | Skin, mucus, cilia, stomach acid, saliva, tears | Instant — blocks entry |
| 2 | Innate cellular defence | Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells phagocytose / kill; inflammation and fever | Minutes to hours |
| 3 | Humoral adaptive immunity | B lymphocytes → plasma cells → antibodies neutralise free antigen | Days on first meeting |
| 4 | Cell-mediated adaptive immunity | Cytotoxic T cells destroy virus-infected and cancer cells; helper T cells coordinate | Days on first meeting |
| 5 | Immunological memory | Memory B and T cells — the basis of vaccination | Hours on re-exposure |

**Innate vs adaptive immunity — classified comparison**

| Feature | Innate immunity | Adaptive immunity |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Present from birth | Develops after exposure to antigen |
| Specificity | Non-specific — attacks anything foreign | Specific to one antigen (epitope) |
| Memory | None — same response every time | Memory cells — faster and stronger on re-exposure |
| Main players | Skin, mucus, acid, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells | B lymphocytes (antibodies), T lymphocytes (helper, cytotoxic) |
| Speed | Immediate | Slow on first exposure (primary), rapid afterwards (secondary) |
| Diversity | Fixed set of receptors | Millions of antigen receptors by rearrangement |

**Cells of the immune system — who does what**

| Cell | Class | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Neutrophil | Innate, phagocyte | First responder; engulfs bacteria at wounds |
| Macrophage | Innate, phagocyte | Engulfs debris and pathogens; presents antigen to T cells |
| Natural killer (NK) cell | Innate, cytotoxic | Kills virus-infected and tumour cells without prior exposure |
| B lymphocyte | Adaptive, humoral | Makes antibodies; becomes memory B cell |
| Helper T cell (CD4) | Adaptive, coordinator | Activates B cells and cytotoxic T cells — the cell HIV destroys |
| Cytotoxic T cell (CD8) | Adaptive, cell-mediated | Punches holes in infected / cancerous cells (perforin) |
| Memory B / T cell | Adaptive, memory | Persists for years; drives the fast secondary response |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example.** A splinter enters the skin. Barriers fail (step 1). Neutrophils and macrophages arrive within hours; the area reddens and swells — inflammation (step 2). Macrophages present antigen to helper T cells, which activate B cells; antibodies appear after ~5–7 days (step 3). Cytotoxic T cells clear any infected cells (step 4). Memory cells persist — a second splinter with the same bacteria is cleared in 1–2 days (step 5).

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Differentiate innate and adaptive immunity in five points. (2) Name the two arms of adaptive immunity and their effector cells. (3) Which cell does HIV attack and why does that collapse the whole adaptive response? (4) What is cell-mediated immunity — give one situation where it matters (transplant rejection, tumour surveillance). (5) Define immunological memory.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Defence is layered: instant barriers, fast non-specific innate cells, then specific adaptive humoral and cell-mediated arms that remember. Vaccination works because of that memory. **Self-check:** can you place neutrophil, B cell, helper T cell and NK cell in the right layer from memory?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Innate (inborn, non-specific, 4 barriers: physical skin/mucus, physiological acid/tears, cellular WBC, cytokine) vs adaptive (acquired, specific, memory) — the two-column contrast is the whole answer.
Trick 2: Cell-mediated (T cells, graft rejection) vs humoral (B cells → antibodies) — name the two arms of adaptive immunity.
Trick 3: Active immunity (own antibodies, slow, long-lasting, vaccination) vs passive (borrowed antibodies, immediate, short, e.g. maternal IgG) — the comparison table.
Trick 4: AIDS attacks helper T cells → both arms fail — the immunology link line.
